key_insight: Although aggregate validation metrics (e.g., perplexity) follow smooth power-law scaling, individual downstream tasks show diverse behaviors — improving, plateauing, or degrading with scale — so validation perplexity alone cannot reliably predict task performance.
problem_solved: Addresses the gap between smooth aggregate neural scaling laws and noisy, heterogeneous downstream task scaling, identifying why validation-perplexity-based predictions fail and what limits simple parametric extrapolation.
method: Empirically analyze how a wide set of individual downstream tasks scale across model/compute regimes and contrast them with aggregate validation loss curves.
Show that averaging token-level losses hides task-specific signals and that no single simple parametric family captures the variety of per-task scaling behaviors.
Propose analyzing finer-grained signals (e.g., token- or task-level decompositions and nonparametric fits) to better characterize and predict downstream performance.
impact: Helps practitioners avoid over-reliance on aggregate perplexity when forecasting model usefulness and motivates task-aware evaluation and modeling strategies for more reliable scaling predictions.
visual_elements: Line chart: smooth power-law curve for aggregate validation loss vs. overlaid diverse per-task curves (improve/plateau/degrade).
Heatmap: tasks (rows) × model scale (columns) showing performance heterogeneity across scales.
Diagram: token-level loss decomposition vs. averaged perplexity to illustrate lost signal from averaging.
Schematic: parametric fit failure — simple curve families vs. actual nonparametric task trajectories.
paper_authors: Michael Y. Hu, Jane Pan, Ayush Rajesh Jhaveri, Nicholas Lourie, Kyunghyun Cho
